Quirk Singularity Theory.text: A fringe theory, discussed more often in pop-science books and late-night talk shows than in policy, holds that Quirks grow stronger, more complex and harder to control with each generation. Its supporters point to children whose powers outstrip both parents', to blended Quirks that combine several family traits, and to the number of young children who need specialist help to keep their Quirks in check. Their prediction is grim: at some point Quirks will outgrow the bodies that carry them, and a generation will be born that cannot control its own powers at all. Most scientists dismiss the theory as alarmism. They note that the data are thin, that strong Quirks are easier to notice than weak ones, and that better counseling and training have kept childhood accidents in check. The theory has no official standing: the government does not plan around it, hero academies do not teach it as fact, and its proponents carry little weight in their fields. It survives on online forums and in the occasional documentary, and people bring it up again whenever a child's Quirk causes a disaster on the evening news. For most people it is an unsettling idea that is easy to set aside.
